title: Caregiving
hookLine: caring for the sick or elderly is holy work
tomorrow: Saba's writing a letter for after he's gone. what goes in it?

lines: THE CLICK OF A PILL ORGANIZER.
cards: Listen to a house where someone is recovering. The click of a pill organizer, its little lids marked with days. A cane tapping down the hall at three in the morning.
A kettle, again. And under all of it, one person who hasn't slept properly in a week and says she's fine. Who takes care of the carer?
The Talmud's answer starts with a broom.

teach.h: AKIVA GOES. THE FLOOR IS SWEPT.
teach.b: In the tractate Nedarim, one of Rabbi Akiva's students falls ill, and none of the sages come to see him. Akiva goes. And because the floor is swept and sprinkled for his visit, the student recovers.
He tells Akiva: you brought me back to life. Not a miracle prayer. A clean floor, and someone who showed up.
The Talmud ties this work to God directly.
In the tractate Sotah, it reads the start of Genesis eighteen, "And the LORD appeared unto him by the terebinths of Mamre," as God visiting Abraham while he was recovering.
And it draws the lesson: just as God visits the sick, so should you.

teach.h: BIKUR CHOLIM: WALK IN GOD'S WAYS.
teach.b: Walk in God's ways. The name for this is bikur cholim, visiting the sick, and it reaches past the patient.
The person changing sheets, counting pills and listening for the cane in the night is doing the same holy work, just without a visit's end.
Which is why carers need carers. A meal on their step.
An hour so they can sleep. A floor swept before they think to ask. Something to tell a friend tonight: in a Talmud story, what helps the sick student recover is a sage who comes, and a swept floor.

how: Jewish communities often organize bikur cholim, visiting and helping the sick, and some synagogues have volunteers who bring meals, give rides, and give caregivers time to rest.

o: a paid nursing job in a hospital or home
looking after the sick or old, as holy work
a prayer said once a year for the sick

games.q: who cared for whom — tap the pairs.
p: went when no one else did

s: in the Talmud story, Rabbi Akiva heals his student with a special prayer
the floor is swept and sprinkled for the visit, and the student recovers. someone showed up.
the Talmud reads Genesis 18 as God visiting Abraham while he recovered
in Sotah: as God visits the sick, so should you.
caring for the sick is a nice extra, not part of walking in God's ways
Sotah lists it among the ways of God that people are asked to follow.

games.q: your neighbor has been caring for her husband after a stroke. you want to help, but you barely know them. what fits the Akiva story?
o: show up with something practical, like a meal or an hour of help.
wait until they ask; offering might be intrusive.
send a long message about how strong she is, and leave it there.
games.why: Akiva went when the others didn't, and a swept floor helped bring his student back. practical presence is the mitzvah.

practice: Do one small, physical act of care near you, slowly: straighten a blanket, wipe a counter, put one thing back where it belongs. Feel your hands doing it.
While you do, picture one person who cares for someone else, and one task you could lift off them this week.

wordCard.voice: Caregiving: the daily, unglamorous work of looking after the sick or the old. The Talmud calls it walking in God's ways.

orig.note: Hebrew: visiting the sick. the mitzvah of caring for those who are ill.

carryVoice: Your line: carers are holy; in the Talmud, even God visits the sick. Rest when you can.
